claims.claim_text: TĀ 2 (Anupāya/No Means chapter): 'Of what use can any means of realization be with regard to this Supreme Lord Who is self-luminous Light and our own Self? It cannot bring about the attainment of His own nature, because it is eternal, nor knowledge of it, because it illumines itself.' From the Anupāya perspective, the two-aspect structure (subject/object, means/goal, ground/grounded) was never truly separate. The reflexivity debate — whether structure is self-grounding (Dignāga), vimarśa-grounded (Abhinavagupta), or groundless (Ñāṇavīra) — operates at the level where separation appears real. Anupāya is the perspective from which the question dissolves.
claims.hetu: consciousness is self-luminous and requires no means — the distinction between ground and grounded does not arise at this level
claims.sadhya: the reflexivity debate presupposes a separation that Anupāya reveals as never having been actual
claims.vyapti_statement: If consciousness needs no means to itself because it IS self-luminous, then the question 'what grounds the two aspects?' is a question that only arises from within the separation it presupposes.

falsifier.condition: Show that the Anupāya perspective still requires the two-aspect distinction (at least as something to be transcended), making it a position within the debate rather than a dissolution of it.
